headline: Clothing workers in Bangladesh strike for higher pay

sources.title: Clothing factories shut in Bangladesh as workers strike over pay (BBC)
Bangladesh garment-makers threaten to quit wage talks (AFP via Yahoo News)
'Going hungry': Garment workers in Bangladesh say wages barely cover needs (Al Jazeera)

chunks.text: A [[sewing worker]] in Bangladesh, a country in South Asia, earns about 121 dollars a month. Her two children {{dropped out}} of school in 2026 because she could not pay for it. She is one of about four million [[garment]] workers, people who make clothes in factories. Since October 31, 2026, many have {{walked out}} of their factories to demand higher pay.

verbs.correct: To stop working as a protest
verbs.wrong: To work extra hours at night

chunks.text: Bangladesh sells more clothes [[abroad]] than any nation except China. Clothing [[exports]] {{make up}} about 80 percent of its sales to other countries. The [[minimum wage]], the lowest monthly pay allowed, has been about 102 dollars since December 2023. Prices have {{gone up}} every year since then. Workers say they cannot {{get by}} because their pay has {{fallen behind}} the cost of food and [[rent]]. They want about 240 dollars, an increase of 140 percent.

verbs.why: My salary falls behind my bills every winter. Pay in many jobs falls behind the cost of living. Workers in Bangladesh say their pay has fallen behind the cost of food and rent.

chunks.text: Factory owners said protests [[disrupted]] work at 529 factories on November 1. That day, the government {{put together}} a [[wage board]], a group led by a judge that recommends new minimum pay. The board said it would {{go over}} the workers' [[demands]] and finish by the end of November. On November 15, workers [[blocked]] a main [[highway]] for about an hour before police {{stepped in}}.

verbs.why: The school puts together a team to plan the trip. The mayor puts together a group to study the bus system. On November 1, 2026, the government of Bangladesh put together a wage board.

verbs.wrong: To hide something from the public
verbs.why: The teacher goes over each test with the class. My boss goes over every report before it is sent. The wage board said it would go over the workers' demands and finish by the end of November.

verbs.correct: To act to stop a problem
verbs.wrong: To fix holes in the road
verbs.why: A teacher steps in when two students argue loudly. The government steps in when a big bank is in trouble. On November 15, workers blocked a main highway for about an hour before police stepped in.

chunks.text: On November 14, the main owners' groups [[threatened]] to {{pull out of}} the board's [[wage talks]] without a promise that factories would be protected. They said factories hit by protests would close and not pay workers, as the [[labor law]] allows. Nearly 150 factories closed that weekend. On November 3, an owners' official warned that big [[pay raises]] could [[cost jobs]] unless the foreign brands that buy the clothes pay [[fairer prices]]. A workers' [[union]] leader {{spoke out}}, saying workers have earned too little for years. The weeks {{leading up to}} Christmas are the [[busiest season]] for exports.

verbs.wrong: To pay the full cost of something
verbs.why: Some players pull out of the game because of injuries. A company pulls out of the deal when the price is too high. The two main factory owners' groups threatened to pull out of the wage talks.

verbs.wrong: To repeat what a boss tells you
verbs.why: Some doctors speak out about unsafe hospital rules. Students speak out when the school cuts sports. A workers' union leader spoke out, saying garment workers have earned too little for years.

verbs.why: Stores get busy in the days that lead up to Thanksgiving. Many students sleep less in the weeks that lead up to exams. The weeks leading up to Christmas are the busiest season for clothing exports from Bangladesh.

mainIdea.s: Clothing workers in Bangladesh went on strike in late October, asking for a much bigger minimum wage. Owners warn of lost jobs, and many factories have closed during the dispute.
mainIdea.why: Workers walked out because their pay has fallen behind prices. Owners say big raises could cost jobs, and nearly 150 factories were closed one weekend.

mainIdea.s: Sewing staff in Bangladesh stopped working after their bosses cut monthly pay in 2026. A new board led by a judge now wants wages returned to the level they had before the cut.
mainIdea.why: Close, but nobody cut their pay. The minimum wage has stayed the same since December 2023, and workers say they cannot get by as prices rise.

mainIdea.s: A large factory group in South Asia has opened free schools for the children of its workers. The owners hope this will help families who cannot pay for classes and keep staff longer.
mainIdea.why: This story is about garment workers who walked out to demand a higher minimum wage, and owners who threatened to quit the wage talks.

tf.why: A leader of a workers' union spoke out, saying workers have earned too little for years while owners and brands make money.

lines.text: Did you see the news about clothing workers in Bangladesh?
A little. They {{walked out}} of their factories, right?
Yes, since late October. They want the minimum wage raised from about 102 dollars a month to about 240.
That's a big jump. Why so much?
They say their pay has {{fallen behind}} the cost of food and rent. Prices have {{gone up}} every year since 2023.
So they can't {{get by}} on what they earn now.
Not really. When you earn about a hundred dollars a month, [[every penny counts]].
It {{put together}} a wage board on November 1. The board will {{go over}} the workers' demands.
And what do the factory owners say?
They say big raises could cost jobs unless brands pay fairer prices. Two owners' groups even threatened to {{pull out of}} the talks.
I agree. A union leader {{spoke out}} and said workers have earned too little for years.
I think they deserve [[a fair shake]].
Me too. But [[there's no easy answer]], because the factories need orders too.
And the weeks {{leading up to}} Christmas are the busiest time for clothing exports.
Right. The next few weeks really matter for everyone.
